statement: For every [space-constructible function](c:space-constructible-function) $f$ with $f(n) \ge \log_2 n$, every language that a [nondeterministic Turing machine](c:nondeterministic-turing-machine) decides in [space](c:space-complexity) $O(f(n))$ is decided by a deterministic Turing machine in space $O(f(n)^2)$: $\mathsf{NSPACE}(f(n)) \subseteq \mathsf{DSPACE}(f(n)^2)$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [space-constructible](c:space-constructible-function): a deterministic machine computes $f(n)$ from $1^n$ in space $O(f(n))$.
The bound satisfies $f(n) \ge \log_2 n$ for all large $n$.

proofs.name: Midpoint recursion on the configuration graph
proofs.slogan: Decide reachability in the configuration graph by recursive midpoint search, so the depth and each frame cost $O(f(n))$ space.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for a machine $M$ that uses space $c\,f(n)$ on inputs of length $n$. First modify $M$ to erase its tape before it accepts, so that it has one accepting configuration.

roles.why: With $f(n) \ge \log n$ the input head position fits in $O(f(n))$ bits, so each configuration has a short code.
The simulator computes $f(n)$ within space $O(f(n))$, so it knows the code length and the recursion depth.

steps.slogan: Encode each [configuration](c:cfg) of $M$ on the input by a string of $O(f(n))$ bits.
steps.detail: A configuration is the state, the work tape content, the work head position and the input head position. Because $f(n) \ge \log n$, it has a code of length $d\,f(n)$, so there are at most $2^{d f(n)}$ configurations. $M$ accepts if and only if the accepting configuration has [reachability](c:reachability) from the start configuration in at most $2^{d f(n)}$ moves.

steps.slogan: Compute $f(n)$ deterministically and fix the depth $k = d\,f(n)$.
steps.detail: Because $f$ is [space-constructible](c:space-constructible-function), the simulator marks off $f(n)$ cells in space $O(f(n))$. This gives the code length and the exponent $k$ of the path bound $2^k$ without writing $2^k$ out.

steps.slogan: Reduce a path of length at most $2^i$ to two paths of length at most $2^{i-1}$.
steps.detail: Let $R(u,v,i)$ say that a path of at most $2^i$ moves leads from $u$ to $v$. Then $R(u,v,0)$ holds when $u = v$ or $v$ follows $u$ in one move, and for $i \ge 1$, $R(u,v,i)$ holds if and only if $R(u,w,i-1)$ and $R(w,v,i-1)$ hold for some configuration $w$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate $R(\mathrm{start},\mathrm{accept},k)$ by a depth-first recursion that reuses its space.
steps.detail: The deterministic procedure tries each $w$ in turn and calls itself twice, and each frame stores only $u$, $v$, $i$ and the current $w$, which is $O(f(n))$ bits. The depth is $k = O(f(n))$, so the total space is $O(f(n)^2)$, and the procedure accepts exactly when $M$ accepts.

concepts.c:space-constructible-function: Constructibility lets the simulator compute its depth within the space budget.
concepts.c:nondeterministic-turing-machine: Its nondeterministic choices become a search for a path of configurations.
concepts.c:space-complexity: Space is the resource that the recursion bounds by $O(f(n)^2)$.
concepts.c:cfg: Configurations are the vertices of the graph that the recursion searches.
concepts.c:reachability: Acceptance is reachability of the accepting configuration from the start.

source.note: The standard proof of W. J. Savitch, Relationships between nondeterministic and deterministic tape complexities, Journal of Computer and System Sciences 4 (1970), 177-192; see M. Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, Theorem 8.5.

statement: Let $X$ be a compact [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) of dimension $n$ with [canonical bundle](c:canonical-bundle) $K_X$, and let $E$ be a [holomorphic vector bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) on $X$. For each $q$, the pairing $(\alpha,\beta) \mapsto \int_X \alpha\wedge\beta$ induces an isomorphism $H^q(X,E) \cong H^{n-q}(X,E^*\otimes K_X)^*$ of finite-dimensional [sheaf cohomology](c:sheaf-cohomology) spaces.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a compact [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) of complex dimension $n$ without boundary.
$E$ is a [holomorphic vector bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) of finite rank on $X$.

conclusion: The integration pairing $H^q(X,E) \times H^{n-q}(X,E^*\otimes K_X) \to \mathbb{C}$ is perfect, so $H^q(X,E) \cong H^{n-q}(X,E^*\otimes K_X)^*$.

proofs.name: Harmonic forms and the Hodge star
proofs.slogan: Represent classes by harmonic Dolbeault forms and pair each harmonic form with its conjugate Hodge star to show that the integration pairing is perfect.
proofs.scope: An outline of the analytic proof; the Hodge theorem for the $\bar\partial$-Laplacian in step 3 rests on the cited work. For $q < 0$ or $q > n$ both sides are zero.

roles.why: Compactness without boundary lets Stokes's theorem remove exact terms and makes the harmonic spaces finite dimensional.
Holomorphy of $E$ gives the operator $\bar\partial_E$ and the Dolbeault complex of $E$-valued forms.

steps.slogan: Replace both cohomology groups by [Dolbeault cohomology](c:dolbeault-cohomology) of bundle-valued forms.
steps.detail: The Dolbeault theorem gives $H^q(X,E) \cong H^{0,q}_{\bar\partial}(X,E)$. An $E^*\otimes K_X$-valued $(0,p)$-form is an $E^*$-valued $(n,p)$-form, so $H^{n-q}(X,E^*\otimes K_X) \cong H^{n,n-q}_{\bar\partial}(X,E^*)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the integration pairing is well defined on cohomology classes.
steps.detail: Contract $E$ with $E^*$ to get an $(n,n)$-form $\alpha\wedge\beta$ and integrate it. If $\alpha = \bar\partial\gamma$ and $\bar\partial\beta = 0$, then $\alpha\wedge\beta = d(\gamma\wedge\beta)$ because $\gamma\wedge\beta$ has type $(n,n-1)$, and Stokes's theorem on the closed manifold gives $\int_X \alpha\wedge\beta = 0$.

steps.slogan: Choose Hermitian metrics and take the harmonic representative of each class.
steps.detail: With metrics on $X$ and $E$, the Laplacian $\Delta = \bar\partial\bar\partial^* + \bar\partial^*\bar\partial$ is elliptic. The cited Hodge theorem says that each class has a unique [harmonic](c:harmonic-form) representative and that the harmonic spaces are finite dimensional.

steps.slogan: Map harmonic $E$-valued forms to harmonic $E^*$-valued forms by the conjugate [Hodge star](c:hodge-star).
steps.detail: The conjugate-linear operator $\bar *_E$ sends $E$-valued $(0,q)$-forms to $E^*$-valued $(n,n-q)$-forms and satisfies $\bar\partial^* = -\bar *\,\bar\partial\,\bar *$. Hence it maps harmonic forms bijectively onto harmonic forms.

steps.slogan: Pair each harmonic form with its star to get a positive number.
steps.detail: For harmonic $\alpha \ne 0$, $\int_X \alpha\wedge\bar *_E\alpha = \|\alpha\|_{L^2}^2 > 0$, so the pairing is nondegenerate in the first slot. Step 4 gives the same in the second slot, and finite dimension turns the nondegenerate pairing into the isomorphism.

concepts.c:complex-manifold: The manifold carries the Dolbeault complex and integration of $(n,n)$-forms.
concepts.c:canonical-bundle: Twisting by $K_X$ turns $(0,p)$-forms into $(n,p)$-forms for the pairing.
concepts.c:holomorphic-vector-bundle: The bundle supplies the operator $\bar\partial_E$ and its dual bundle.
concepts.c:sheaf-cohomology: Both sides of the duality are sheaf cohomology groups.
concepts.c:dolbeault-cohomology: Dolbeault classes are forms that can be wedged and integrated.
concepts.c:harmonic-form: Harmonic representatives make the positivity argument possible.
concepts.c:hodge-star: The conjugate Hodge star gives each class its dual partner.

source.ref: D. Huybrechts, Complex Geometry: An Introduction, Universitext, Springer, Berlin, 2005, Section 4.1, Proposition 4.1.15
source.note: The proof by harmonic forms and the conjugate Hodge star, with the Hodge theorem for bundle-valued forms in the same section. The algebraic version over any field is proved in R. Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry, Springer, 1977, Section III.7.

statement: On a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$, the map $A \mapsto (e^{itA})_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$ is a bijection from the [self-adjoint operators](c:self-adjoint-operator) on $H$, possibly unbounded, onto the strongly continuous one-parameter groups of [unitary operators](c:unitary-operator). The inverse sends $U$ to its generator $A\psi = \lim_{t\to0}(U_t\psi - \psi)/(it)$, defined on the vectors $\psi$ where this limit exists.

hypotheses.text: In the forward direction, $A$ is a [self-adjoint operator](c:self-adjoint-operator) on $H$.
In the converse direction, each $U_t$ is [unitary](c:unitary-operator), $U_0 = I$ and $U_{s+t} = U_sU_t$.
In the converse direction, $t \mapsto U_t\psi$ is continuous for every $\psi \in H$.

conclusion: Each $e^{itA}$ is a strongly continuous unitary group with generator $A$, and every such group equals $e^{itA}$ for exactly one self-adjoint $A$.

proofs.name: Functional calculus and the generator
proofs.slogan: Build $e^{itA}$ by the spectral theorem, and show conversely that the generator of a unitary group is densely defined and self-adjoint and generates the group.
proofs.scope: Both directions and injectivity. Unbounded $A$ is the main case; a bounded $A$ gives a norm-continuous group.

roles.why: Self-adjointness gives a [spectral measure](c:spectral-measure), which defines $e^{itA}$ and identifies its generator.
The group law and unitarity give $U_t^* = U_{-t}$, which makes the generator symmetric and drives the deficiency argument.
Strong continuity makes the smoothed vectors $\int f(t)U_t\psi\,dt$ exist and converge to $\psi$, and makes orbits differentiable on the domain.

steps.slogan: Define $U_t = e^{itA}$ by integration against the [spectral measure](c:spectral-measure) of $A$.
steps.detail: The spectral theorem gives $A = \int\lambda\,dE(\lambda)$, and $U_t = \int e^{it\lambda}\,dE(\lambda)$ is a unitary group because $|e^{it\lambda}| = 1$ and $e^{i(s+t)\lambda} = e^{is\lambda}e^{it\lambda}$. Strong continuity follows from $\|U_t\psi - \psi\|^2 = \int|e^{it\lambda} - 1|^2\,d\mu_\psi$ and dominated convergence.

steps.slogan: Show that the generator of $e^{itB}$ is exactly $B$ for self-adjoint $B$.
steps.detail: For $\psi \in D(B)$, $\|(U_t\psi - \psi)/(it) - B\psi\|^2 = \int|(e^{it\lambda}-1)/(it) - \lambda|^2\,d\mu_\psi \to 0$ by dominated convergence with bound $4\lambda^2$. If the limit exists, Fatou's lemma gives $\int\lambda^2\,d\mu_\psi < \infty$, so $\psi \in D(B)$. Hence $A \mapsto e^{itA}$ is injective.

steps.slogan: Smooth vectors by $\psi_f = \int f(t)U_t\psi\,dt$ to show that the generator is densely defined.
steps.detail: For $f \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$, $(U_s\psi_f - \psi_f)/s = \int\frac{f(t-s) - f(t)}{s}U_t\psi\,dt \to -\psi_{f'}$, so $\psi_f \in D(A)$; also $U_t$ maps $D(A)$ into itself. An approximate identity $f$ gives $\psi_f \to \psi$, so $D(A)$ is [dense](c:dense-set).

steps.slogan: Show that $A$ is symmetric and that $A^*\varphi = \pm i\varphi$ forces $\varphi = 0$.
steps.detail: From $U_t^* = U_{-t}$ one gets $\langle A\varphi,\psi\rangle = \langle\varphi,A\psi\rangle$ on $D(A)$. If $A^*\varphi = i\varphi$, then $g(t) = \langle U_t\psi,\varphi\rangle$ satisfies $g' = g$ for $\psi \in D(A)$, so the bounded $g$ vanishes and $\varphi \perp D(A)$, hence $\varphi = 0$; the case $-i$ is the same. So the closure $\bar A$ is self-adjoint.

steps.slogan: Compare $U_t$ with $e^{it\bar A}$ and conclude that $U_t = e^{itA}$ with $A$ self-adjoint.
steps.detail: For $\psi \in D(A)$, $w(t) = U_t\psi - e^{it\bar A}\psi$ satisfies $w' = i\bar A w$ and $w(0) = 0$, so $\frac{d}{dt}\|w\|^2 = 2\operatorname{Re}\langle i\bar Aw,w\rangle = 0$ and $w = 0$. By density $U_t = e^{it\bar A}$, and step 2 shows that its generator $A$ equals $\bar A$.

concepts.c:hilbert-space: The inner product gives adjoints, unitarity and the norm identity for $w$.
concepts.c:self-adjoint-operator: Self-adjoint operators are the generators in the correspondence.
concepts.c:unitary-operator: Unitary groups form the other side of the bijection.
concepts.c:spectral-measure: The spectral measure defines $e^{itA}$ and computes its generator.
concepts.c:dense-set: A densely defined generator has an adjoint, which the deficiency argument needs.

source.note: The standard proof in M. Reed and B. Simon, Methods of Modern Mathematical Physics I: Functional Analysis, Academic Press, 1980, Theorems VIII.7 and VIII.8.

statement: Let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group), $p$ a prime and $|G| = p^a m$ with $p \nmid m$. Then $G$ has a subgroup of order $p^k$ for every $p^k \mid |G|$; every [p-subgroup](c:p-group) lies in a [Sylow subgroup](c:sylow-subgroup), of order $p^a$; all Sylow $p$-subgroups are [conjugate](c:conjugate-subgroup); and their number $n_p$ satisfies $n_p \equiv 1 \pmod p$ and $n_p \mid m$.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group).
$p$ is a prime number.

conclusion: Subgroups of every order $p^k$ dividing $|G|$ exist, Sylow $p$-subgroups contain every $p$-subgroup up to conjugacy and are all conjugate, and $n_p \equiv 1 \pmod p$ with $n_p \mid m$.

formal.difference: The declaration proves only the first part: a subgroup of order $p^n$ for each $p^n$ dividing $|G|$. Conjugacy and the count are the separate declarations Sylow.isPretransitive_of_finite, card_sylow_modEq_one and Sylow.card_dvd_index.

proofs.name: Growing p-subgroups and counting fixed points
proofs.slogan: Grow a $p$-subgroup one factor of $p$ at a time inside its normalizer, then let $p$-groups act on cosets and on Sylow subgroups and count fixed points modulo $p$.
proofs.scope: All three parts. For $a = 0$ the Sylow subgroup is trivial and $n_p = 1$, and the arguments still apply.

roles.why: Finiteness makes all orbit and coset counts finite numbers that can be reduced modulo $p$.
Primality makes every nontrivial orbit of a $p$-group have size divisible by $p$, and it gives Cauchy's theorem.

steps.slogan: Count the fixed points of a [p-group](c:p-group) action modulo $p$.
steps.detail: Let a $p$-group $P$ [act](c:group-action) on a finite set $X$. Each orbit has size $[P : P_x]$, a power of $p$, so $|X| \equiv |X^P| \pmod p$, where $X^P$ is the set of fixed points.

steps.slogan: Enlarge a subgroup of order $p^k$ to one of order $p^{k+1}$ inside its [normalizer](c:normalizer).
steps.detail: Let $|H| = p^k$ with $p^{k+1} \mid |G|$, and let $H$ act on $G/H$ by left multiplication; the fixed cosets form $N(H)/H$. Step 1 gives $[N(H):H] \equiv [G:H] \equiv 0 \pmod p$, so Cauchy's theorem gives a subgroup of order $p$ in $N(H)/H$, whose preimage has order $p^{k+1}$. Induction from $H = \{1\}$ gives part 1.

steps.slogan: Let a $p$-subgroup act on the cosets of a Sylow subgroup and find a fixed coset.
steps.detail: Let $S$ be a [Sylow subgroup](c:sylow-subgroup) from step 2 and let a $p$-subgroup $P$ act on $G/S$, a set of size $m \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$. Step 1 gives a fixed coset $gS$, so $P \le gSg^{-1}$. If $P$ is Sylow, then $P = gSg^{-1}$ by order, which gives part 2.

steps.slogan: Let a Sylow subgroup act on all Sylow subgroups by conjugation and show that it fixes only itself.
steps.detail: If $S$ normalizes the Sylow subgroup $T$, then $S$ and $T$ are Sylow subgroups of $N(T)$, so step 3 makes them [conjugate](c:conjugate-subgroup) in $N(T)$. Since $T$ is normal in $N(T)$, $S = T$. Step 1 then gives $n_p \equiv 1 \pmod p$.

steps.slogan: Compute $n_p$ as an index and remove the factor $p^a$.
steps.detail: By step 3, $G$ acts transitively on the Sylow subgroups by conjugation with stabilizer $N(S)$, so $n_p = [G:N(S)]$ divides $|G| = p^a m$. Step 4 makes $n_p$ prime to $p$, so $n_p \mid m$.

concepts.c:finite-group: All counts are finite and can be reduced modulo $p$.
concepts.c:p-group: Orbits of a $p$-group have $p$-power sizes, which drives every count.
concepts.c:sylow-subgroup: Sylow subgroups are the maximal $p$-subgroups that the proof builds and counts.
concepts.c:conjugate-subgroup: Conjugation permutes the Sylow subgroups transitively.
concepts.c:normalizer: The normalizer holds the fixed cosets and is the conjugation stabilizer.
concepts.c:group-action: Each part comes from a well-chosen action of a $p$-group.

source.note: mathlib grows a subgroup of order $p^n$ to order $p^{n+1}$ (Sylow.exists_subgroup_card_pow_succ) with IsPGroup.card_modEq_card_fixedPoints, fixedPointsMulLeftCosetsEquivQuotient and Cauchy's theorem exists_prime_orderOf_dvd_card'. Steps 3 to 5 follow Sylow.isPretransitive_of_finite, card_sylow_modEq_one and Sylow.card_dvd_index.

statement: For a set $P$ of $n$ points and a set $L$ of $m$ lines in the Euclidean plane, the number $I$ of incidences, the pairs $(p,\ell)$ with $p \in P$, $\ell \in L$ and $p \in \ell$, satisfies $I \le 4\,n^{2/3}m^{2/3} + 4n + m$. In particular $I = O(n^{2/3}m^{2/3} + n + m)$.

hypotheses.text: $P$ is a set of $n$ distinct points and $L$ a set of $m$ distinct lines in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

proofs.name: Crossing-number proof
proofs.slogan: Turn the incidences into a drawn graph whose crossings are few because two lines meet at most once, and compare with the crossing lemma.
proofs.scope: The whole bound with the stated constants; if $n = 0$ or $m = 0$ then $I = 0$. The matching lower bound from a grid example is not part of this statement.

roles.why: Distinct lines meet in at most one point, and two distinct points lie on one line only, so the drawn graph is simple and has few crossings.

steps.slogan: Join consecutive points on each line to form a drawn graph.
steps.detail: Let $G$ have vertex set $P$, and on each line join consecutive points of $P$ by the segment between them. A line with $k \ge 1$ points gives $k - 1$ edges, so $G$ has $e \ge I - m$ edges, and no edge repeats because two points lie on one line only.

steps.slogan: Bound the crossings of any drawing below by $e - 3v$.
steps.detail: A simple [planar graph](c:planar-graph) with $v$ vertices has at most $3v$ edges by Euler's formula. Deleting one edge for each crossing leaves a planar drawing, so every drawing of a simple graph has at least $e - 3v$ crossings.

steps.slogan: Sample the vertices at random to raise the lower bound to $e^3/(64v^2)$.
steps.detail: Keep each vertex with probability $q$ and apply step 2 to the induced drawing. A crossing uses four distinct vertices, so taking [expectations](c:expected-value) gives $q^4\,\mathrm{cr} \ge q^2 e - 3qv$. With $q = 4v/e \le 1$ when $e \ge 4v$, this gives the [crossing number](c:crossing-number) bound $\mathrm{cr} \ge e^3/(64v^2)$.

steps.slogan: Bound the crossings of the drawing above by $m^2$.
steps.detail: Two crossing edges lie on two different lines, and two different lines meet in at most one point. So the drawing has at most $\binom{m}{2} \le m^2$ crossings.

steps.slogan: Combine the two crossing bounds in two cases.
steps.detail: If $e < 4n$, then $I < 4n + m$. Otherwise steps 3 and 4 give $(I - m)^3/(64n^2) \le e^3/(64n^2) \le m^2$, so $I \le 4\,n^{2/3}m^{2/3} + m$. In both cases $I \le 4\,n^{2/3}m^{2/3} + 4n + m$.

concepts.c:planar-graph: Euler's formula for planar graphs gives the base crossing bound.
concepts.c:expected-value: Linearity of expectation amplifies the weak bound by random sampling.
concepts.c:crossing-number: The crossing lemma ties the number of edges to the number of crossings.

source.note: L. A. Székely, Crossing numbers and hard Erdős problems in discrete geometry, Combinatorics, Probability and Computing 6 (1997), 353-358; the crossing lemma is due to Ajtai, Chvátal, Newborn and Szemerédi and to Leighton.

statement: Let $T$ be a [consistent theory](c:consistent-theory) in the language of arithmetic that contains [Robinson arithmetic](c:robinson-arithmetic) $Q$. No formula $\tau(x)$ satisfies $T \vdash \varphi \leftrightarrow \tau(\ulcorner\varphi\urcorner)$ for every sentence $\varphi$, where $\ulcorner\varphi\urcorner$ is the [Gödel number](c:godel-numbering) of $\varphi$. With $T$ the true sentences of $\mathbb{N}$: arithmetical truth is not definable in arithmetic.

hypotheses.text: $T$ is [consistent](c:consistent-theory).
$T$ proves every axiom of [Robinson arithmetic](c:robinson-arithmetic) $Q$.

conclusion: No arithmetic formula $\tau(x)$ is a truth predicate for $T$; in particular no formula defines the set of Gödel numbers of sentences true in $\mathbb{N}$.

proofs.name: Liar sentence from the diagonal lemma
proofs.slogan: Build by the diagonal lemma a sentence that says of itself that it is not true, which makes any truth predicate inconsistent.
proofs.scope: The syntactic form; the semantic form follows with $T = \mathrm{Th}(\mathbb{N})$, which is consistent and contains $Q$ because $\mathbb{N}$ is a model of both.

roles.why: Robinson arithmetic represents the computable diagonal function, which the diagonal lemma needs.
A theory that proves $\lambda \leftrightarrow \neg\lambda$ is inconsistent, which contradicts this hypothesis.

steps.slogan: Represent the diagonal function on [Gödel numbers](c:godel-numbering) by a formula of arithmetic.
steps.detail: The map $d$ that sends the code of a formula $\psi(x)$ to the code of $\psi(\ulcorner\psi\urcorner)$ is computable. Every computable function is representable in $Q$, so a formula $\delta(x,y)$ satisfies $Q \vdash \forall y\,(\delta(\overline{k},y) \leftrightarrow y = \overline{d(k)})$ for each $k$.

steps.slogan: Build the liar sentence $\lambda$ with $T \vdash \lambda \leftrightarrow \neg\tau(\ulcorner\lambda\urcorner)$.
steps.detail:
Let $	heta(x) = \exists y\,(\delta(x,y) \wedge 
eg	au(y))$ and $\lambda = 	heta(\ulcorner	heta\urcorner)$. Then $d(\ulcorner	heta\urcorner) = \ulcorner\lambda\urcorner$, and step 1 gives $T \vdash \lambda \leftrightarrow 
eg	au(\ulcorner\lambda\urcorner)$. This is the diagonal lemma for the formula $
eg	au(x)$.

steps.slogan: Instantiate the assumed truth predicate at the liar sentence.
steps.detail: If $T \vdash \varphi \leftrightarrow \tau(\ulcorner\varphi\urcorner)$ for every sentence $\varphi$, then $T \vdash \lambda \leftrightarrow \tau(\ulcorner\lambda\urcorner)$. With step 2 this gives $T \vdash \lambda \leftrightarrow \neg\lambda$.

steps.slogan: Derive both $\lambda$ and $\neg\lambda$ and contradict consistency.
steps.detail: From $\lambda \leftrightarrow \neg\lambda$, propositional logic proves both $\lambda$ and $\neg\lambda$, so $T$ is inconsistent. This contradicts the hypothesis, so no such $\tau$ exists; for $T = \mathrm{Th}(\mathbb{N})$, a formula that defines truth would be such a $\tau$.

concepts.c:consistent-theory: Consistency is what the liar sentence contradicts.
concepts.c:robinson-arithmetic: This weak theory already represents the diagonal function.
concepts.c:godel-numbering: Coding lets a formula speak about sentences through numbers.

source.note: The standard diagonal-lemma proof of A. Tarski, Der Wahrheitsbegriff in den formalisierten Sprachen, Studia Philosophica 1 (1936); it appears in standard logic texts such as H. B. Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic.

statement: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of closed [balls](c:ball) $\bar B(x,r)$, $r \ge 0$, in a [metric space](c:metric-space), with bounded radii. Then $\mathcal{F}$ has a pairwise disjoint subfamily $\mathcal{G}$ such that every $\bar B(x,r) \in \mathcal{F}$ meets some $\bar B(y,s) \in \mathcal{G}$ with $r \le 2s$, and hence $\bar B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(y,5s)$.

hypotheses.text: Each member of $\mathcal{F}$ is a closed [ball](c:ball) $\bar B(x,r)$ with $r \ge 0$ in a [metric space](c:metric-space) $X$.
The radii are bounded: $\sup\{r : \bar B(x,r) \in \mathcal{F}\} < \infty$.

conclusion: A disjoint subfamily $\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{F}$ satisfies $\bigcup\mathcal{F} \subseteq \bigcup_{\bar B(y,s) \in \mathcal{G}} \bar B(y,5s)$.

formal.difference: The declaration is the measure-theoretic Vitali covering theorem that this lemma feeds: from a fine family of closed sets with a doubling bound it extracts a countable disjoint subfamily that covers almost all of a set. The lemma itself is Vitali.exists_disjoint_subfamily_covering_enlargement_closedBall, with any factor $\tau > 3$ in place of $5$.

proofs.name: Zorn on good disjoint families
proofs.slogan: Take by Zorn's lemma a maximal disjoint family in which every ball that meets the family meets a comparable member, and show that maximality leaves no ball out.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma with ratio $2$; any ratio $\tau > 1$ works the same way and gives the factor $1 + 2\tau$. An empty family gives $\mathcal{G} = \emptyset$.

roles.why: A meeting point of two balls and the triangle inequality turn a meeting with a larger ball into containment in its enlargement.
Bounded radii give a finite supremum of the radii of the balls that miss the family.

steps.slogan: Call a disjoint subfamily good when each ball that meets it meets a member at least half as large.
steps.detail: A subfamily $\mathcal{U}$ is good if its balls are pairwise disjoint and every $\bar B(x,r) \in \mathcal{F}$ that meets a member of $\mathcal{U}$ meets some $\bar B(y,s) \in \mathcal{U}$ with $r \le 2s$. The empty family is good.

steps.slogan: Choose a maximal good family by Zorn's lemma for inclusion.
steps.detail: The union of a [chain](c:chain) of good families is good: two of its balls lie in one member of the chain, so they are disjoint, and a witness in one member stays in the union. Zorn's lemma gives a maximal good family $\mathcal{G}$.

steps.slogan: Show that every ball meets $\mathcal{G}$ by adding a large missing ball otherwise.
steps.detail: Suppose the set $\mathcal{A}$ of balls that miss all of $\mathcal{G}$ is nonempty; let $M < \infty$ be the supremum of their radii and pick $B' \in \mathcal{A}$ with radius $s' > M/2$, or any $B'$ if $M = 0$. A ball that meets $B'$ either meets $\mathcal{G}$ or lies in $\mathcal{A}$ with radius $\le M \le 2s'$, so $\mathcal{G} \cup \{B'\}$ is good, which contradicts maximality.

steps.slogan: Enlarge the comparable member by the triangle inequality.
steps.detail: Each $\bar B(x,r) \in \mathcal{F}$ meets $\mathcal{G}$ by step 3, so by goodness it meets some $\bar B(y,s) \in \mathcal{G}$ with $r \le 2s$. For $z$ in $\bar B(x,r)$, $d(z,y) \le 2r + s \le 5s$, so $\bar B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(y,5s)$.

concepts.c:ball: The lemma selects disjoint balls and enlarges them by the factor $5$.
concepts.c:metric-space: The triangle inequality of the metric gives the enlargement bound.
concepts.c:chain: Zorn's lemma needs an upper bound for every chain of good families.

source.note: The linked declaration Vitali.exists_disjoint_covering_ae starts from this lemma. mathlib proves Vitali.exists_disjoint_subfamily_covering_enlargement by zorn_subset on the good families and deduces the closed-ball form.

proofs.name: Greedy selection by radius layers
proofs.slogan: Sort the balls into layers of comparable radius and choose maximal disjoint subfamilies layer by layer, from the largest radii down.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma; balls of radius $0$ form a last layer that is treated in the same way. In a separable space each choice is a countable greedy induction; in general it uses Zorn's lemma.

roles.why: The triangle inequality turns a meeting with a ball of at least half the radius into containment in its $5$-fold enlargement.
A finite $R = \sup r$ puts every positive radius into some layer $R/2^{j+1} < r \le R/2^j$.

steps.slogan: Split the family into layers of radii between $R/2^{j+1}$ and $R/2^j$.
steps.detail: Let $R = \sup r < \infty$ and $\mathcal{F}_j = \{\bar B(x,r) \in \mathcal{F} : R/2^{j+1} < r \le R/2^j\}$ for $j \ge 0$. Every ball of positive radius lies in exactly one layer.

steps.slogan: Choose a maximal disjoint subfamily of each layer that avoids the earlier choices.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal{G}_j$ be a maximal disjoint subfamily of the balls in $\mathcal{F}_j$ that miss every ball of $\mathcal{G}_0 \cup \dots \cup \mathcal{G}_{j-1}$. Such families exist by Zorn's lemma, and $\mathcal{G} = \bigcup_j \mathcal{G}_j$ is disjoint.

steps.slogan: Show that each ball of layer $j$ meets a chosen ball of radius above $R/2^{j+1}$.
steps.detail: If $B \in \mathcal{F}_j$ missed all of $\mathcal{G}_0, \dots, \mathcal{G}_j$, it could be added to $\mathcal{G}_j$, which contradicts maximality. So $B$ meets some $\bar B(y,s) \in \mathcal{G}_i$ with $i \le j$, and $s > R/2^{i+1} \ge R/2^{j+1} \ge r/2$.

steps.slogan: Enlarge the met ball by the triangle inequality.
steps.detail: With $r \le 2s$ and a common point of $\bar B(x,r)$ and $\bar B(y,s)$, every $z \in \bar B(x,r)$ satisfies $d(z,y) \le 2r + s \le 5s$. So $\bar B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(y,5s)$.

concepts.c:ball: The layers sort balls by radius, and the chosen balls are enlarged by $5$.
concepts.c:metric-space: The triangle inequality of the metric gives the enlargement bound.

source.note: The layer-by-layer selection as in L. C. Evans and R. F. Gariepy, Measure Theory and Fine Properties of Functions, CRC Press, 1992, Section 1.5.1.

statement: Let $f\colon X \to Y$ be a map between connected [CW complexes](c:cw-complex). If $f_*\colon \pi_n(X,x_0) \to \pi_n(Y,f(x_0))$ is an isomorphism of [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group) for every $n \ge 1$, that is, $f$ is a [weak homotopy equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence), then $f$ is a [homotopy equivalence](c:homotopy-equivalence).

hypotheses.text: $X$ and $Y$ are connected [CW complexes](c:cw-complex).
$f_*\colon \pi_n(X,x_0) \to \pi_n(Y,f(x_0))$ is an isomorphism for every $n \ge 1$.

conclusion: Some map $g\colon Y \to X$ satisfies $g \circ f \simeq \mathrm{id}_X$ and $f \circ g \simeq \mathrm{id}_Y$.

proofs.name: Mapping cylinder and compression
proofs.slogan: Replace $f$ by the inclusion of $X$ into its mapping cylinder, show that the relative homotopy groups vanish, and compress the cylinder onto $X$ cell by cell.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; for disconnected complexes apply it to each component when $f$ is a bijection on components. When $f$ is the inclusion of a subcomplex, steps 3 and 4 alone suffice.

roles.why: The CW structure makes $f$ cellular up to homotopy and lets the compression go one cell at a time.
The isomorphisms make the relative homotopy groups of the cylinder vanish.

steps.slogan: Make $f$ cellular and form its [mapping cylinder](c:mapping-cylinder) $M_f$.
steps.detail: By cellular approximation $f$ is homotopic to a [cellular map](c:cellular-map), and the conclusion is invariant under homotopy, so assume $f$ cellular. Then $M_f$ is a CW complex with $X$ and $Y$ as subcomplexes, and it has a [deformation retraction](c:deformation-retract) $r\colon M_f \to Y$ with $r|_X = f$.

steps.slogan: Show that the [relative homotopy groups](c:relative-homotopy-group) $\pi_n(M_f, X)$ vanish.
steps.detail: The inclusion $i\colon X \to M_f$ satisfies $r \circ i = f$, and $r$ is a homotopy equivalence, so $i_*$ is an isomorphism on every $\pi_n$. The long exact sequence of the pair $(M_f, X)$ then gives $\pi_n(M_f, X) = 0$ for all $n \ge 1$.

steps.slogan: Compress a map of a CW pair into the subspace one cell at a time.
steps.detail: Let $(W,A)$ be a CW pair and $\phi\colon (W,A) \to (Z,B)$ with $\pi_n(Z,B) = 0$ for all $n$. By induction over the cells of $W \setminus A$, each $n$-cell gives an element of $\pi_n(Z,B)$, which is zero, so $\phi$ on that cell deforms into $B$ rel its boundary; the homotopy extension property extends each deformation over $W$.

steps.slogan: Deform the cylinder onto $X$ by compressing its identity map.
steps.detail: Step 2 allows step 3 for $\mathrm{id}\colon (M_f, X) \to (M_f, X)$. This gives a homotopy rel $X$ from the identity to a retraction $\rho\colon M_f \to X$, so $X$ is a deformation retract of $M_f$ and $i$ is a homotopy equivalence.

steps.slogan: Compose the two homotopy equivalences to recover $f$.
steps.detail: Since $f = r \circ i$ with $i$ and $r$ homotopy equivalences, $f$ is a [homotopy equivalence](c:homotopy-equivalence). A homotopy inverse is $g = \rho \circ j$, where $j\colon Y \to M_f$ is the inclusion.

concepts.c:cw-complex: The cells give the induction that compresses the cylinder.
concepts.c:homotopy-group: Isomorphisms on homotopy groups are the hypothesis that the theorem upgrades.
concepts.c:weak-homotopy-equivalence: This names the hypothesis; the theorem promotes it on CW complexes.
concepts.c:homotopy-equivalence: This is the conclusion, built from the cylinder.
concepts.c:mapping-cylinder: The cylinder turns $f$ into the inclusion of a subcomplex.
concepts.c:cellular-map: A cellular map has a mapping cylinder that is a CW complex.
concepts.c:deformation-retract: The cylinder retracts onto $Y$, and compression retracts it onto $X$.
concepts.c:relative-homotopy-group: Their vanishing is exactly what the compression needs.

source.note: A. Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Cambridge University Press, 2002, Theorem 4.5 with the compression Lemma 4.6.

statement: Let $a_i, a_i^\dagger$ satisfy the [canonical commutation relations](c:canonical-commutation-relation), and let $\phi_1,\dots,\phi_m,\psi_1,\dots,\psi_n$ be linear combinations of them. With [normal ordering](c:normal-ordering) $:\;:$ and contraction $\langle\phi\psi\rangle = \phi\psi - {:}\phi\psi{:}$, the product ${:}\phi_1\cdots\phi_m{:}\,{:}\psi_1\cdots\psi_n{:}$ equals $\sum_M \prod_{(i,j)\in M}\langle\phi_i\psi_j\rangle\,{:}\prod_{i\notin M}\phi_i\prod_{j\notin M}\psi_j{:}$ over all partial matchings $M$ between the $\phi_i$ and the $\psi_j$.

hypotheses.text: The operators satisfy $[a_i,a_j^\dagger] = \delta_{ij}$ and $[a_i,a_j] = [a_i^\dagger,a_j^\dagger] = 0$.
Each $\phi_i$ and $\psi_j$ is a finite linear combination of the [creation and annihilation operators](c:creation-and-annihilation-operators).

conclusion: The product of two normal-ordered monomials is the sum, over all partial matchings between them, of the product of the matched contractions times the normal-ordered product of the unmatched factors.

proofs.name: Moving annihilators to the right
proofs.slogan: Split each field into creation and annihilation parts, move the annihilation parts of the left factor to the right, and collect one scalar contraction per swap.
proofs.scope: The whole formula for bosonic [free field](c:free-field) modes; for $m = 0$ or $n = 0$ only the empty matching occurs and the formula is trivial. Fermionic fields give the same formula with signs.

roles.why: The relations make each commutator of an annihilation part with a creation part a scalar, and make like parts commute.
Linearity lets each field split into one creation part and one annihilation part.

steps.slogan: Split each field into its creation part and its annihilation part.
steps.detail: Write $\phi = \phi^+ + \phi^-$, with $\phi^+$ a combination of the $a_i^\dagger$ and $\phi^-$ of the $a_i$. Then $\langle\phi\psi\rangle = \phi^-\psi^+ - \psi^+\phi^- = [\phi^-,\psi^+]$ is a scalar, and creation parts commute with each other, as do annihilation parts.

steps.slogan: Expand each normal-ordered monomial as a sum over subsets.
steps.detail: Normal ordering puts creation parts to the left, so ${:}\phi_1\cdots\phi_m{:} = \sum_S \prod_{i\in S}\phi_i^+\prod_{i\notin S}\phi_i^-$ over subsets $S \subseteq \{1,\dots,m\}$. The same holds for the $\psi_j$ with subsets $T$.

steps.slogan: Move one annihilation part past a product of creation parts.
steps.detail: Because $[c,\cdot\,]$ is a derivation and each $[c,b_j]$ is a scalar, $c\,b_1\cdots b_k = b_1\cdots b_k\,c + \sum_j [c,b_j]\prod_{l\ne j}b_l$. Each term either moves $c$ to the far right or removes $c$ and one $b_j$ for a scalar factor.

steps.slogan: Induct on the number of annihilation parts to get a sum over matchings.
steps.detail: Applying step 3 to each annihilation part in turn gives $\prod_{i\in A}\phi_i^-\prod_{j\in B}\psi_j^+ = \sum_M \prod_{(i,j)\in M}[\phi_i^-,\psi_j^+]\prod_{j\in B\setminus M}\psi_j^+\prod_{i\in A\setminus M}\phi_i^-$ over partial matchings $M$ of $A$ with $B$. Induction on $|A|$ proves this.

steps.slogan: Regroup the terms by matching to rebuild the normal-ordered product.
steps.detail: Insert step 4 into the product of the expansions of step 2; every term is now normal ordered. For a fixed matching $M$, the sum over the choices for the unmatched factors rebuilds ${:}\prod_{i\notin M}\phi_i\prod_{j\notin M}\psi_j{:}$ by step 2, with coefficient $\prod_{(i,j)\in M}\langle\phi_i\psi_j\rangle$ by step 1.

concepts.c:canonical-commutation-relation: The relations make every contraction a scalar.
concepts.c:creation-and-annihilation-operators: Each field splits into one creation and one annihilation part.
concepts.c:normal-ordering: Normal order is the form in which both sides are written.
concepts.c:free-field: Free-field modes obey exactly these commutation relations.

source.note: The standard induction on annihilation operators, after G. C. Wick, The evaluation of the collision matrix, Physical Review 80 (1950), 268-272.

statement: Let $\Phi$ be a nonvanishing function on $\mathbb{R}$ with $\Phi(\pm\infty) = 1$, Hölder continuous on $\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}$, with [winding number](c:winding-number) $0$ about the origin. Then $\Phi = \Phi_+\Phi_-$ on $\mathbb{R}$, where $\Phi_\pm$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) and nonvanishing in the upper or lower [half-plane](c:half-plane), continuous up to $\mathbb{R}$ and equal to $1$ at infinity. This [factorization](c:factorization) is unique.

hypotheses.text: $\Phi\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$ is continuous, never zero, and $\Phi(x) \to 1$ as $x \to \pm\infty$.
$\Phi$ is Hölder continuous on the circle $\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}$.
The closed curve $\Phi(\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\})$ has [winding number](c:winding-number) $0$ about $0$.

conclusion: There are unique $\Phi_+$ and $\Phi_-$, holomorphic and nonvanishing in the upper and lower half-planes, continuous up to $\mathbb{R}$, tending to $1$ at infinity, with $\Phi = \Phi_+\Phi_-$ on $\mathbb{R}$.

proofs.name: Logarithm and Cauchy integrals
proofs.slogan: Take a logarithm of the function, split it additively with Cauchy integrals and the Plemelj formulas, and exponentiate the two parts.
proofs.scope: Existence and uniqueness under the stated normalization. A nonzero winding number $\kappa$ adds a factor $((x-i)/(x+i))^{\kappa}$ and is excluded here.

roles.why: A nonvanishing function has a continuous logarithm, and the limit $1$ at infinity fixes it to be $0$ at one end.
Winding number zero makes the continuous logarithm return to $0$ at the other end.
Hölder continuity makes the Cauchy integrals have continuous boundary values that obey the Plemelj formulas.

steps.slogan: Choose a continuous [logarithm](c:logarithm) $L$ of $\Phi$ that vanishes at infinity.
steps.detail: Because $\Phi$ never vanishes, a continuous branch $L = \log\Phi$ exists on $\mathbb{R}$ with $L(-\infty) = 0$, and $L(+\infty) - L(-\infty)$ is $2\pi i$ times the winding number, which is $0$. $L$ is Hölder on $\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}$ because $\log$ is Lipschitz near the compact image of $\Phi$.

steps.slogan: Split $L$ into upper and lower parts by the Cauchy integral.
steps.detail: Set $L_\pm(z) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{L(t)}{t-z}\,dt$ for $\pm\operatorname{Im} z > 0$. These are holomorphic and tend to $0$ at infinity, and by the Sokhotski–Plemelj theorem their boundary values are continuous and satisfy $L_+(x) - L_-(x) = L(x)$ on $\mathbb{R}$.

steps.slogan: Exponentiate the two parts to get the factors.
steps.detail: Put $\Phi_+ = e^{L_+}$ and $\Phi_- = e^{-L_-}$. They are holomorphic and nonvanishing in their half-planes, continuous up to $\mathbb{R}$, tend to $1$ at infinity, and $\Phi_+\Phi_- = e^{L_+ - L_-} = e^{L} = \Phi$ on $\mathbb{R}$.

steps.slogan: Glue the quotients of two factorizations into a bounded entire function.
steps.detail: If also $\Phi = \Psi_+\Psi_-$, then $\Phi_+/\Psi_+ = \Psi_-/\Phi_-$ on $\mathbb{R}$. The function equal to the left side above $\mathbb{R}$ and the right side below is continuous across $\mathbb{R}$, so Morera's theorem makes it [entire](c:entire-function); it is bounded with limit $1$, so Liouville's theorem makes it $1$.

concepts.c:winding-number: Index zero lets the logarithm vanish at both ends of the line.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: The two factors must be holomorphic in opposite half-planes.
concepts.c:half-plane: Each factor and each Cauchy integral lives on one half-plane.
concepts.c:factorization: The theorem writes the function as a product of two one-sided factors.
concepts.c:logarithm: The logarithm turns the product problem into an additive splitting problem.
concepts.c:entire-function: Gluing the two quotients gives an entire function for Liouville's theorem.

source.note: The classical Cauchy-integral construction, as in F. D. Gakhov, Boundary Value Problems, Pergamon, 1966, and B. Noble, Methods Based on the Wiener-Hopf Technique, Pergamon, 1958.

statement: Assume the [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice). If every [chain](c:chain) in a [partially ordered set](c:partial-order) $P$ has an [upper bound](c:upper-bound) in $P$, then $P$ has a [maximal element](c:maximal-element): some $m \in P$ such that no $a \in P$ satisfies $m < a$.

hypotheses.text: Every [chain](c:chain) $C \subseteq P$, the empty chain included, has an upper bound in $P$.
The [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice) holds.

conclusion: Some $m \in P$ satisfies $m \le a \Rightarrow a = m$ for every $a \in P$.

formal.difference: The declaration works for any transitive relation $\prec$ and gives $m$ with $m \prec a \Rightarrow a \prec m$, which is maximality for a partial order. Choice is built into Lean's logic, so it is not a hypothesis there.

proofs.name: Upper bound of a maximal chain
proofs.slogan: Take a maximal chain, take an upper bound of it, and show that nothing lies strictly above that bound.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma. The empty chain has an upper bound, so $P$ is nonempty.

roles.why: Choice builds the maximal chain through the Hausdorff maximal principle.
The maximal chain has an upper bound.

steps.slogan: Choose a maximal chain $C$ by the Hausdorff maximal principle.
steps.detail: The Hausdorff maximal principle gives a chain $C \subseteq P$ that lies in no strictly larger chain. mathlib builds $C$ as the closure of the empty chain under unions and a successor map that a choice function picks.

steps.slogan: Take an upper bound $m$ of the maximal chain.
steps.detail: By hypothesis the chain $C$ has an [upper bound](c:upper-bound) $m \in P$. So $c \le m$ for every $c \in C$.

steps.slogan: Add any element above $m$ to the chain and keep a chain.
steps.detail: Let $m \le a$. Every $c \in C$ satisfies $c \le m \le a$, so by transitivity $C \cup \{a\}$ is still a [chain](c:chain).

steps.slogan: Use maximality of the chain to force $a = m$.
steps.detail: Maximality of $C$ gives $C \cup \{a\} = C$, so $a \in C$ and therefore $a \le m$. With $m \le a$, antisymmetry gives $a = m$, so $m$ is a [maximal element](c:maximal-element).

concepts.c:axiom-of-choice: Choice supplies the selections that build the maximal element.
concepts.c:chain: Chains are the subsets whose upper bounds the hypothesis supplies.
concepts.c:partial-order: Antisymmetry and transitivity of the order are used in the final step.
concepts.c:upper-bound: Bounds of chains are the raw material for the maximal element.
concepts.c:maximal-element: A maximal element is what the lemma produces.

source.note: mathlib takes the maximal chain maxChain with maxChain_spec, built from a chosen successor map (the Hausdorff principle), bounds it by the hypothesis, and closes with IsChain.insert and maximality.

proofs.name: Transfinite recursion
proofs.slogan: If no element were maximal, choose strict upper bounds again and again along the ordinals and get an injection of all ordinals into a set.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma by contradiction, in ZFC.

roles.why: Choice picks one strict upper bound for every chain at once.
Each chain has an upper bound, which becomes a strict bound when no element is maximal.

steps.slogan: Assume that no element is maximal and choose a strict upper bound for every chain.
steps.detail: If no element is maximal, each chain $C$ has an upper bound $u$ and some $u' > u$, which is a strict upper bound of $C$. The axiom of choice gives a function $g$ with $c < g(C)$ for every chain $C$ and every $c \in C$.

steps.slogan: Define $a_\alpha = g(\{a_\beta : \beta < \alpha\})$ by transfinite recursion.
steps.detail: By [transfinite induction](c:transfinite-induction) on the [ordinal](c:ordinal) $\alpha$, the set $\{a_\beta : \beta < \alpha\}$ is a chain with $a_\beta < a_\gamma$ for $\beta < \gamma < \alpha$. So $g$ applies to it, and $a_\alpha$ lies strictly above every earlier term.

steps.slogan: Show that $\alpha \mapsto a_\alpha$ injects all ordinals into $P$ and derive a contradiction.
steps.detail: Strict increase makes the map injective on the class of all ordinals. By replacement on its image, a subset of $P$, the ordinals would form a set, which contradicts the Burali-Forti paradox.

concepts.c:axiom-of-choice: Choice supplies the selections that build the maximal element.
concepts.c:chain: Chains are the subsets whose upper bounds the hypothesis supplies.
concepts.c:partial-order: Antisymmetry and transitivity of the order are used in the final step.
concepts.c:upper-bound: Bounds of chains are the raw material for the maximal element.
concepts.c:maximal-element: A maximal element is what the lemma produces.
concepts.c:transfinite-induction: Transfinite recursion builds the strictly increasing sequence.
concepts.c:ordinal: The sequence is indexed by all ordinals, too many for a set.

source.note: The classical proof by transfinite recursion, as in T. Jech, Set Theory, Springer, 2003, Chapter 5.

statement: Let $\sum_{n\ge0} a_n$ be a convergent series of complex numbers with sum $l$, and let $f(z) = \sum a_n z^n$ be its [power series](c:power-series) on $|z| < 1$. Then $f(z) \to l$ as $z \to 1$ inside any [Stolz angle](c:stolz-angle) $S_M = \{z : |z| < 1,\ |1-z| < M(1-|z|)\}$; in particular $f(x) \to l$ as $x \to 1^-$.

hypotheses.text: The [partial sums](c:partial-sum) $s_N = \sum_{n<N} a_n$ converge to $l$.
The point $z$ stays in a fixed [Stolz angle](c:stolz-angle) $S_M$ with $M > 1$.

formal.difference: The declaration takes the approach region to be the cone $|\operatorname{Im} z| < s(1 - \operatorname{Re} z)$, which near $1$ lies inside some Stolz set $S_M$. The Stolz set form is Complex.tendsto_tsum_powerSeries_nhdsWithin_stolzSet.

proofs.name: Summation by parts
proofs.slogan: Write $l - f(z)$ as $(1-z)$ times a power series in the tails $l - s_{n+1}$, then bound its head by $|1-z|$ and its tail by the Stolz angle.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The real case follows because $[0,1)$ lies in $S_M$ for every $M > 1$.

roles.why: Convergence makes the tails $l - s_{n+1}$ bounded, and small beyond some index $N$.
In $S_M$ the ratio $|1-z|/(1-|z|)$ stays below $M$, which controls the tail.

steps.slogan: Rewrite $l - f(z)$ as $(1-z)\sum_n (l - s_{n+1}) z^n$ by summation by parts.
steps.detail: For $|z| < 1$, summation by parts gives $f(z) = (1-z)\sum_n s_{n+1} z^n$, and $l = (1-z)\sum_n l\,z^n$. Subtraction gives $l - f(z) = (1-z)\sum_n (l - s_{n+1}) z^n$; the series converges because the tails are bounded.

steps.slogan: Split the series at an index $N$ beyond which the tails are below $\varepsilon$.
steps.detail: Given $\varepsilon > 0$, convergence of the [partial sums](c:partial-sum) gives $N$ with $|l - s_{n+1}| < \varepsilon$ for $n \ge N$. Write the series as a head over $n < N$ and a tail over $n \ge N$.

steps.slogan: Bound the tail by $\varepsilon M$ inside the Stolz angle.
steps.detail: The tail has modulus at most $\varepsilon|1-z|\sum_n |z|^n = \varepsilon|1-z|/(1-|z|)$. Inside the [Stolz angle](c:stolz-angle) $S_M$ this is less than $\varepsilon M$.

steps.slogan: Bound the head by a constant times $|1-z|$.
steps.detail: Since $|z|^n \le 1$, the head has modulus at most $|1-z|\,C_N$ with $C_N = \sum_{n<N}|l - s_{n+1}|$. This tends to $0$ as $z \to 1$.

steps.slogan: Combine both bounds and let $\varepsilon$ tend to zero.
steps.detail: For $z \in S_M$ with $|1-z| < \varepsilon/(C_N+1)$, $|l - f(z)| \le |1-z|\,C_N + \varepsilon M < (M+1)\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, $f(z) \to l$ inside $S_M$.

concepts.c:power-series: The theorem concerns the boundary behaviour of a power series at $z = 1$.
concepts.c:stolz-angle: The angle keeps $|1-z|/(1-|z|)$ bounded, which controls the tail.
concepts.c:partial-sum: The tails of the partial sums become the new coefficients.

source.note: mathlib reduces the cone to a Stolz set (nhdsWithin_stolzCone_le_nhdsWithin_stolzSet) and proves tendsto_tsum_powerSeries_nhdsWithin_stolzSet from the rearrangement abel_aux, splitting the sum at an index as here.

statement: Let $D$ be a [complete](c:complete-category), [locally small](c:locally-small) category and $G\colon D \to C$ a functor. Then $G$ has a left [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) if and only if $G$ preserves small [limits](c:limit-category-theory) and satisfies the [solution set condition](c:solution-set-condition): for each object $c$ of $C$, some set of arrows $f_i\colon c \to Gd_i$ lets every $h\colon c \to Gd$ factor as $h = G(t)\circ f_i$.

hypotheses.text: $D$ has all small limits.
$D$ is [locally small](c:locally-small): each class of arrows $D(x,y)$ is a set.

conclusion: $G$ is a right adjoint exactly when it preserves small limits and has solution sets.

proofs.name: Initial objects of comma categories
proofs.slogan: Build an initial object of each comma category $c \downarrow G$ from a weakly initial product and a joint equalizer, then assemble these objects into a left adjoint.
proofs.scope: Both directions; the last step proves the easy direction. The category $C$ is arbitrary.

roles.why: Completeness of $D$ makes each comma category complete, so products and equalizers exist there.
Local smallness makes the endomorphisms of the weakly initial product a set, so their joint equalizer exists.

steps.slogan: Show that the [comma category](c:comma) $c \downarrow G$ is complete and locally small.
steps.detail: Its objects are arrows $c \to Gd$. A limit of a diagram of such arrows is the limit $\lim d_i$ in $D$ with the induced arrow $c \to G(\lim d_i) \cong \lim Gd_i$, which exists because $G$ preserves limits. Its hom-sets are subsets of hom-sets of $D$.

steps.slogan: Take the product of the solution set as a weakly initial object.
steps.detail: The arrows $f_i$ form a set of objects of $c \downarrow G$, and every object receives an arrow from one of them. Their product $P$ in $c \downarrow G$ therefore maps to every object, so $P$ is weakly initial.

steps.slogan: Equalize all endomorphisms of $P$ to get an initial object.
steps.detail: Let $e\colon E \to P$ be the joint [equalizer](c:equalizer) of all endomorphisms of $P$; $E$ maps to every object through $P$. If $u, v\colon E \to x$ have equalizer $k$ and $s\colon P \to \mathrm{dom}\,k$, then $eks$ is an endomorphism, so $ekse = e$ and $kse = 1_E$ because $e$ is monic. So $k$ is split epi, $u = v$, and $E$ is an [initial object](c:initial-object).

steps.slogan: Assemble the initial objects of the comma categories into a left adjoint.
steps.detail: An initial object $\eta_c\colon c \to G(Fc)$ of $c \downarrow G$ is a universal arrow, and a left adjoint is the same as a choice of universal arrow for every $c$. Universality defines $F$ on arrows and gives $D(Fc,d) \cong C(c,Gd)$ naturally.

steps.slogan: Prove the converse from the universal arrows of a given left adjoint.
steps.detail: If $F \dashv G$, the unit $\eta_c$ alone is a solution set, since $h = G(h^\flat)\circ\eta_c$. The natural bijection $C(c, G\lim d_i) \cong D(Fc, \lim d_i) \cong \lim C(c, Gd_i)$ and the Yoneda lemma show that $G$ preserves limits.

statement: A ring $R$ is [semisimple](c:semisimple-ring) if and only if $R \cong M_{n_1}(D_1) \times \cdots \times M_{n_k}(D_k)$ for some $k \ge 0$, integers $n_i \ge 1$ and [division rings](c:division-ring) $D_i$. The number $k$ and the pairs $(n_i, D_i)$ are unique up to order and isomorphism of the $D_i$. In particular a simple [Artinian ring](c:artinian-ring) is a [matrix ring](c:matrix-ring) $M_n(D)$.

hypotheses.text: For the forward direction, $R$ is semisimple: as a left module over itself it is a direct sum of [simple](c:is-simple-module) left ideals.

conclusion: Semisimple rings are exactly the finite products of matrix rings over division rings, and $R$ determines the factors.

formal.difference: The declaration treats only a simple Artinian algebra and gives $R \cong M_n(D)$ without uniqueness. The product form is IsSemisimpleRing.exists_algEquiv_pi_matrix_divisionRing; neither states the converse or the uniqueness.

proofs.name: Endomorphisms of the regular module
proofs.slogan: Split $R$ into blocks of isomorphic simple left ideals and compute $R^{op} \cong \mathrm{End}_R(R)$ as a product of matrix rings by Schur's lemma.
proofs.scope: Existence, the converse, uniqueness and the simple Artinian case. The zero ring is the empty product with $k = 0$.

roles.why: Semisimplicity splits the regular module $_RR$ into simple left ideals.

steps.slogan: Show that a simple Artinian ring is semisimple with one simple type.
steps.detail: An Artinian ring has a minimal left ideal $I$. The sum of the left ideals $Ia$, $a \in R$, is a nonzero two-sided ideal, so it is $R$, and each $Ia$ is zero or isomorphic to $I$. So $_RR$ is a sum of copies of $I$, hence semisimple with $k = 1$.

steps.slogan: Split $R$ into finitely many simple left ideals and group them by type.
steps.detail: Write $_RR = \bigoplus_\lambda I_\lambda$ with [simple](c:is-simple-module) left ideals; the element $1$ has finitely many nonzero components, and they generate $R$, so the sum is finite. Grouping isomorphic summands gives $_RR \cong S_1^{n_1} \oplus \cdots \oplus S_k^{n_k}$ with pairwise non-isomorphic simple modules $S_i$.

steps.slogan: Compute the maps between simple modules by Schur's lemma.
steps.detail: A nonzero map between simple modules has zero kernel and full image, so it is an isomorphism. Hence $E_i = \mathrm{End}_R(S_i)$ is a [division ring](c:division-ring) and $\mathrm{Hom}_R(S_i, S_j) = 0$ for $i \ne j$.

steps.slogan: Identify $R^{op}$ with $\mathrm{End}_R(R)$ and compute it as a product of matrix rings.
steps.detail: Right multiplications give $R^{op} \cong \mathrm{End}_R(_RR)$. By step 3 an endomorphism of $\bigoplus_i S_i^{n_i}$ is a family of $n_i \times n_i$ matrices over $E_i$, so the [endomorphism ring](c:endomorphism-ring) is $\prod_i M_{n_i}(E_i)$. Transposition gives $R \cong \prod_i M_{n_i}(D_i)$ with $D_i = E_i^{op}$.

steps.slogan: Show that each $M_n(D)$ is semisimple by splitting it into columns.
steps.detail: As a left module, $M_n(D)$ is the direct sum of its $n$ columns, each isomorphic to $D^n$, and $D^n$ is simple because matrices move any nonzero vector to any vector. A finite product of semisimple rings is semisimple, since its regular module is the sum of those of the factors.

steps.slogan: Recover $k$, the $n_i$ and the $D_i$ from the simple modules of $R$.
steps.detail: For $R \cong \prod_i M_{n_i}(D_i)$, step 5 shows that the simple $R$-modules are the column modules $D_i^{n_i}$, pairwise non-isomorphic since different factors annihilate them. So $k$ is the number of simple types, $n_i$ is the multiplicity of the $i$-th type in $_RR$, and $D_i \cong \mathrm{End}_R(D_i^{n_i})^{op}$, as in step 4.

concepts.c:artinian-ring: The Artinian condition gives the minimal left ideal in the simple case.
concepts.c:is-simple-module: Simple left ideals are the building blocks of the decomposition.
concepts.c:endomorphism-ring: The ring is recovered as the opposite of its endomorphism ring.

statement: In an election candidate $A$ receives $p$ votes and candidate $B$ receives $q$ votes, with $p > q \ge 0$. If all orders of counting the $p + q$ ballots are equally likely, then the probability that $A$ is strictly ahead of $B$ throughout the count is $\frac{p-q}{p+q}$.

hypotheses.text: The vote totals satisfy $p > q \ge 0$.
The counting order has the [uniform distribution](c:uniform-distribution) on the $\binom{p+q}{q}$ possible orders.

conclusion: The probability that $A$ stays strictly ahead during the whole count is $(p-q)/(p+q)$.

proofs.name: Reflection of bad orders
proofs.slogan: Count the bad counting orders by reflecting the part before the first tie, which pairs bad orders that start with $A$ with orders that start with $B$.
proofs.scope: All $p > q \ge 0$; for $q = 0$ there are no bad orders and the probability is $1$.

roles.why: With $p > q$ the path ends above $0$, so every path that starts with $B$ meets $0$ again, which the reflection needs.
Equally likely orders turn the probability into a ratio of counts.

steps.slogan: Encode each counting order as a path of the running vote difference.
steps.detail: Record $+1$ for an $A$ ballot and $-1$ for a $B$ ballot; the partial sums form a [random walk](c:random-walk) path from $0$ to $p - q$. There are $\binom{p+q}{q}$ equally likely paths, and an order is good when every partial sum after the start is positive.

steps.slogan: Count the orders that start with a $B$ ballot.
steps.detail: Every order whose first ballot is $B$ is bad, because the first partial sum is $-1$. There are $\binom{p+q-1}{q-1}$ such orders, a [binomial coefficient](c:binomial-coefficient) that counts the places of the other $q - 1$ ballots for $B$.

steps.slogan: Reflect a bad path that starts with $A$ up to its first zero.
steps.detail: A bad path that starts with $+1$ returns to $0$ at a first time $\tau$. Negating the steps before $\tau$ gives a path that starts with $-1$ and has the same end. This is a bijection onto the paths that start with $-1$, because each of them must cross $0$ before it reaches $p - q > 0$.

steps.slogan: Subtract the bad orders and divide by the total.
steps.detail: The bad orders number $2\binom{p+q-1}{q-1}$, and $\binom{p+q-1}{q-1} = \frac{q}{p+q}\binom{p+q}{q}$. So the probability of a good order is $1 - \frac{2q}{p+q} = \frac{p-q}{p+q}$.

concepts.c:uniform-distribution: Uniformity makes the probability a ratio of path counts.
concepts.c:random-walk: The vote difference is a walk, and a good order keeps it positive.
concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: Paths with fixed numbers of steps are counted by binomial coefficients.

source.note: The reflection argument usually credited to D. André (1887); see W. Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 1, Chapter III.

proofs.name: Induction on the last ballot
proofs.slogan: Condition on the last ballot counted and check that $(p-q)/(p+q)$ satisfies the resulting recursion.
proofs.scope: Induction on $p + q$ over all pairs $p \ge q \ge 0$ with $p + q \ge 1$, where the case $p = q$ has probability $0$ and agrees with the formula.

roles.why: The final margin $p - q > 0$ makes the last partial sum positive, so only the earlier count matters.
Under the uniform order the last ballot is for $A$ with probability $p/(p+q)$, and the earlier ballots stay uniform.

steps.slogan: Check the formula in the boundary cases $q = 0$ and $p = q$.
steps.detail: If $q = 0$, $A$ is always ahead, and $(p-0)/(p+0) = 1$. If $p = q$, the count ends in a tie, so $A$ is not strictly ahead throughout, and the formula gives $0$.

steps.slogan: Condition on the last ballot to get a recursion for the probability $P(p,q)$.
steps.detail: The last ballot is for $A$ with [conditional probability](c:conditional-probability) $p/(p+q)$, and given that, the first $p+q-1$ ballots form a uniform order of $p - 1$ and $q$ votes. Since the final margin is positive, $A$ stays ahead exactly when $A$ stays ahead in that shorter count. So $P(p,q) = \frac{p}{p+q}P(p-1,q) + \frac{q}{p+q}P(p,q-1)$.

steps.slogan: Verify that $(p-q)/(p+q)$ satisfies the recursion and close the induction.
steps.detail: With the induction hypothesis, the right side is $\frac{p}{p+q}\cdot\frac{p-1-q}{p+q-1} + \frac{q}{p+q}\cdot\frac{p-q+1}{p+q-1} = \frac{(p-q)(p+q-1)}{(p+q)(p+q-1)} = \frac{p-q}{p+q}$. The base cases of step 1 start the induction.

concepts.c:uniform-distribution: Uniformity is kept when the last ballot is removed.
concepts.c:conditional-probability: Conditioning on the last ballot splits the probability into two cases.

source.note: The standard induction on the number of ballots, by conditioning on the last ballot counted.
